The formal surname of ‘Khazadsson’ or ‘Khazadsdottir’ is used in the extremely rare occurrences where a newborn Dwarf is a foundling of unknown descent. Once the foundling is adopted by another Dwarf, the youngling adds another name consisting of the foster parent’s name with the suffix ‘sfind’ (found by). For example, the foundling Dwarf named Grim and raised by Kazran Moreksson would be Grim Khazadsson-Kazransfind.

When they come of age, Imperial Dwarf foundlings may opt to petition the elders of their adopted clan to change their surname. Usually, these foundlings replace their adopted surname with the (Reikspiel equivalent of) their clan name. In extremely rare cases, Imperial Dwarf clans may decide to go it alone without a surname until they can earn a surname through deed or achievement.

name: Physical Attributes
text:
Determining physical attributes is also important in developing a Dwarf Character. The following table expands on the information in the WFRP Rulebook (pages 40).

Dwarfs have a wide distribution along the Mountains from ranging from Dwarf holds overlooking the arid and Greenskin-infested Badlands to those enduring the cold winds of Norsca. Traits such as hair and eye colour differ between these far-flung lands.

As most Dwarf Characters would come from lands between these extremes, there is a reasonable distribution of such traits. For Norse Dwarf Characters, subtract 5% from each of the dice rolls for hair and eye colour. For Dwarf Characters from the Vaults, Black Mountains, Tilea, and southern Worlds Edge Mountains add 5 to the dice rolls.

The optional column for Distinguished Features does not require a modified roll. This roll is intended to give a Dwarf Character a distinguishing attribute to help the Character stand out (and, perhaps, provide a basis for a nickname). Dwarf Characters should have no more than one of these features, but the Game Master may allow more in order to create an interesting Character.

name: Dwarf Random Class And Career Table
Dwarf Random Class And Career Table
Dwarf Career Updates
text:
This section includes updates to the core Careers in Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay, which apply when a Dwarf Character enters that Career. It includes new Career levels to replace levels in the original Career, to reflect the unique way in which Dwarfs practise that Career. These alternate Career levels are optional — Dwarf Characters can still use the levels printed in WFRP if they choose, or even pay the usual XP cost to Change to a New Level (WFRP Core Rulebook) and acquire both the original and alternate versions of that Career level. Unless otherwise stated, alternate Career levels have the same corresponding Characteristic as the Career level they replace.

Example: Kala has completed her Student Engineer Career, and is Changing to a New Level. She could choose to become an Engineer (WFRP Core Rulebook) or Guild Engineer (page 56), both the second level of her current Career. Either way, the new Characteristic she can purchase Advances for is Initiative.

Later, Kala completes the second level of her Career as a Guild Engineer, and Changes to a New Level again. She could become a Master Engineer, Outcast Engineer, Pilot, or even an Engineer (since she skipped that level to become a Guild Engineer). She chooses to become a Pilot — per the rules for that Career level, she can now buy Advances for the Agility Characteristic, but not Toughness.

name: Reading New Careers
text:
The Careers in this book use a mix of Talents from WFRP and from the new Talents list on pages 80-83. For ease of reference, Talents which are new to this book are denoted with an asterisk (*).

The new Careers also denote some Trappings in italics. These indicate that the Trappings are required for a Character to perform their Career to minimum standard of quality. If a Character’s Required Trappings are lost or destroyed, the Character is ineligible to Earn Money until they are recovered, repaired, or repurchased. A Character without their Required Trappings may even be forced to change to a lower Career level, at the GM’s discretion.

name: Dwarf Rogues
text:
Dwarfs that criminally profit from the hard work of their fellow clansfolk do not last long in the Karaks. A life of crime is anathema to the tenets of oath-keeping, honest labour, community spirit, and obedience of elders that all clans teach their beardlings from a young age.

That said, whilst Dwarfs place a high value on the legal traditions of their ancestors, they are far less minded to observe the corrupt, byzantine, unjust legal systems of the Empire and other nations. It is therefore not uncommon for Dwarfs working abroad to be labelled as criminals. A Dwarf can be branded a Thief for retaking stolen treasures; a Fence for returning those treasures to rightful owners; an Outlaw for soliciting mountain “tolls” not approved by local authorities; or a Racketeer for using force to collect outstanding debts.

When a Dwarf Character acquires the Criminal Talent, they can choose whether its effects apply whilst visiting Dwarf settlements. If not, the Character does not generate increased Income when Earning money in Dwarf settlements, but also avoids the increased scrutiny of its occupants (which can be extremely hostile).

name: Dwarf Trappings
text:
Dwarfs are notoriously proud of their wargear, ensuring that it is of the highest quality and embellished in accordance with their clan’s wealth. Dwarfs prefer the dependable surety of thick steel, shields, sturdy weapons, and thundering missile volleys to the duelling sabre, longbow, or unreliable minds of animal steeds. As such, many of the Trappings awarded as part of a Career may not be appropriate for a Dwarf Character.

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Hand Weapon as a Career Trapping may replace it with a Dwarf Axe or a Dwarf Warhammer.

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Cavalry, Fencing, or Parry weapon as a Career Trapping may replace it with a Shield or a Pistol with ammunition.

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Bow Weapon as a Career Trapping may replace the weapon and its ammunition with a Dwarf Crossbow and ammunition or a Dwarf Handgun and ammunition.

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Riding Horse or Warhorse as a Career Trapping may replace it with Full Plate Armour and a Helm.

A Dwarf Character may also choose to exchange their Career’s weapon Skill Specialisations to match the alternate Trapping options above — for example, a Dwarf Hunter could take Ranged (Crossbow or Blackpowder) as a Career Skill instead of Ranged (Bow).

name: Guild Engineer
text:
War machines are a staple of Dwarfen throngs, and Guild Engineers train not just to assemble these devices, but accompany them into battle. Between campaigns, they assemble and supervise the industry of the Karaks, like water pumps, steam engines, and mining drills.

Guild Engineers replace the 2nd level of the Engineer (WFRP Core Rulebook) or Artillerist (Up In Arms page 18) Career.

Guild Engineer — Silver 3 Skills: Dodge, Drive, Melee (Any One), Ranged (Any One), Research, Trade (Any One) Talents: Craftsman (Engineer), Crew Commander*, Entrenchment*, Orientation Trappings: Trade Tools (Engineer), Dwarf Hammer or Dwarf Greathammer, Dwarf Handgun or Dwarf Pistol, Gromril Suit, Telescope

name: Outcast Engineer
text:
Those who challenge the Engineers Guild’s hidebound conservatism are fated to undergo an elaborate exiling ritual. Despite the shame, many still practise their calling independently. Some even earn their way back into the Guild, though most inventors are only vindicated long after their death.

Outcast Engineers replace the 3rd level of the Engineer (WFRP Core Rulebook) or Artillerist (Up In Arms page 18) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Fellowship.

Outcast Engineer — Silver 3 Skills: Bribery, Entertain, Gamble, Trade (Any One) Talents: Argumentative, Dragon Belcher*, Master Tradesman (Engineer), Sniper Trappings: Dwarf Axe or Dwarf Greataxe, Repeating Dwarf Handgun, Mark of Shame

name: Sky Pilot
text:
Gyrocopters and other skycraft are still distrusted by the Guild’s elders, but many of the most daring Engineers are experts at maintaining and piloting them. Even the most disapproving Dwarf generals can appreciate the tactical advantage of reconnaissance from a bird’s eye view.

Sky Pilots replace the 3rd level of the Engineer (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Agility.

Sky Pilot — Silver 3 Skills: Charm, Navigation, Outdoor Survival, Sail (Skycraft) Talents: Acute Sense (Sight), Maverick*, Seasoned Traveller, Short Fuse* Trappings: Pilot’s Licence, Dwarf Pistol, Telescope

name: Grudgemaster
text:
Sometimes known as Grudgekeepers, these scholars are the ultimate authorities on grudges and proportionate restitution, per the precedent set by revered ancestors. They may dictate the wording of grudges for their Kings to inscribe, or even be empowered to update their Karak’s Book of Grudges personally.

Grudgemasters replace the 3rd level of the Lawyer (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career.

Grudgemaster — Gold 1 Skills: Intuition, Language (Any One), Lore (Any One), Secret Signs (Guilder) Talents: Ancestral Grudge*, Bookish, Long Memory*, Supportive Trappings: Research Archive, Beardling Apprentice, Key to the Hall of Remembering

name: Reckoner
text:
Reckoners are intermediaries who carry records of outstanding grudges between clans and holds. Where possible, they negotiate settlements on their clients’ behalf, expunging grudges for later ratification. Traditionally their logs are inscribed on stone tablets, and shattered upon resolution.

Reckoners replace the 2nd level of the Lawyer (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career.

Reckoner — Silver 4 Skills: Athletics, Evaluate, Intimidate, Lore (Heraldry or History), Navigation, Stealth (Underground) Talents: Dealmaker, Menacing, Sturdy, Tireless* Trappings: Reckoner’s Log, 1d10 Shattered Tablets, Runescribing Kit, Dwarf Axe or Dwarf Hammer, Breastplate, Mail Skirt, Plate Helm (Open)

name: Stoneshaper
text:
Stoneshapers are a combination of mason, architect, and combat engineer, specialising in the construction of stone fortifications. They often supervise excavation work, as they are famed for their instinctive ability to anticipate rockfalls, earthquakes, and other underground disasters. Stoneshapers replace the 2nd level of the Artisan (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Initiative.

Stoneshaper — Silver 1 Skills: Climb, Language (Guilder), Lore (Geology), Navigation, Set Trap, Stealth (Underground) Talents: Enclosed Fighter, Entrenchment*, Sixth Sense, Tireless* Trappings: Trade Tools (Mason), Dwarf Hammer

name: Karak Miner
text:
When called to war, the warriors of the Miner’s Guild fight as they work — wielding picks, and travelling underground. By swiftly digging new tunnels, they undermine and outmanoeuvre their enemies, surprising foes who expected to fight a static and reactionary battleline.

Karak Miners replace the 2nd level of the Miner (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career.

Karak Miner — Silver 1 Skills: Climb, Entertain (Singing), Evaluate, Ranged (Explosives), Secret Signs (Miner), Stealth (Underground) Talents: Enclosed Fighter, Night Vision, Strider (Rocky), Underminer* Trappings: Dwarf Pick, Miner’s Helm, Davrich Lamp, Candle, Lamp Oil, Breastplate, Mail Skirt

name: Lodefinder
text:
The elite of the mining clans are known by many names, including Lodefinders and Lodewardens. Their ability to sniff out valuable deposits is legendary, and they are often trusted to drive or operate advanced mining engineering equipment.

Lodefinders replace the 3rd level of the Miner (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career.

Lodefinder — Silver 2 Skills: Drive, Lore (Geology), Melee (Engineering), Navigation Talents: Detect Artefact, Orientation, Short Fuse*, Tunnel Rat Trappings: Steam Drill, Blasting Charge, Beardling Apprentice

name: Runebearer
text:
Runebearers are long-distance runners who deliver vital messages between holds. Though expected to cross any terrain necessary to reach their destination, they specialise in navigating the tunnels of the Underway. Every Runebearer dreams of setting a new record on the Kislev Run, the longest distance ever travelled in a single mission.

Runebearers replace the 2nd level of the Messenger (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career.

Runebearer — Silver 1 Skills: Cool, Melee (Basic), Ranged (Crossbow), Secret Signs (Ranger), Stealth (Any One), Swim Talents: Orientation, Seasoned Traveller, Strider (Rocky), Tireless* Trappings: Dwarf Axe, Dwarf Crossbow and Ammunition, Leather Jack

name: Slayers Do Not Wear Armour
text:
Slayer Characters cannot ever choose to wear or carry protective wargear. Doing so would risk robbing themselves of the glorious death they crave above all else. More importantly, it would violate their Slayer Oath to Grimnir, mortally dishonouring themselves a second time over, with a shame not even the Slayer Oath can redeem.

Slayers may change Careers as they acquire new expertise — perhaps studying under Malakai Makaisson to become an Outcast Engineer (page 56), or joining the Slayer-Captain Long Drong’s crew of Pirates (Sea of Claws page 78). But even as the Character changes Career, their Slayer Oath remains binding. They are still oathsworn to forsake shields and armour, even if they acquire them as Trappings from their new Careers.

If a player is considering playing a Slayer, but finds the ban on wearing armour to be restrictive, frustrating, or an unacceptable constraint on character agency, the solution is simple: play a different Career. There are many Career options, in this book and others, that provide the opportunity to play a powerful, armoured, monster-slaying warrior that should be more in line with their tastes. The Slayer Career provides a more unusual gameplay challenge, in line with their more unusual character perspective. Embrace that challenge only if you are enthusiastic to do so with sincerity!

name: Axefighter
text:
Many Dwarfs consider the axe the only fitting weapon for a true warrior, and by long tradition regiments of Dwarfs go to battle carrying axes as their primary weapon, preferring the heft and hitting power of a solid war axe over the finesse of a sword blade.

Axefighters replace the 2nd level of the Soldier (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Strength.

Axefighter — Silver 3 Skills: Consume Alcohol, Gamble, Intimidate, Melee (Two-handed), Outdoor Survival, Ranged (Throwing) Talents: Demolisher*, Drilled, Shieldsman, Tireless* Trappings: Dwarf Axe or Dwarf Greataxe, Shield, Breastplate, Mail Skirt, Plate Helm (Open)

name: Quarreller
text:
Crossbows are the traditional Dwarf hunting weapon — more sturdy than bows, and more reliable than blackpowder. Disciplined ranks of Quarrellers have formed the basis of throng firing lines for millennia, standing up far better in melee than most armies’ missile troops.

Quarrellers replace the 2nd level of the Soldier (WFRP Core Rulebook) Career.

Quarreller — Silver 3 Skills: Consume Alcohol, Gamble, Intimidate, Melee (Two-handed), Outdoor Survival, Ranged (Crossbow) Talents: Drilled, Harpooner*, Rapid Reload, Tireless* Trappings: Dwarf Crossbow and Ammunition, Breastplate, Mail Skirt, Plate Helm (Open)

name: Thunderer
text:
Still considered new-fangled after centuries of use, Dwarf handguns are far more precise and reliable than Imperial counterparts. Their wielders are well-named, for the cacophonous roar of a Thunderer’s missile volley is terrifying enough to put survivors to flight.

Thunderers replace the 2nd level of the Soldier (WFRP Core Rulebook) or Handgunner (Up In Arms page 16) Career.

Thunderer — Silver 3 Skills: Evaluate, Gamble, Intimidate, Outdoor Survival, Ranged (Engineering), Trade (Gunsmith) Talents: Dragon Belcher*, Drilled, Tireless*, Unshakeable Trappings: Dwarf Handgun and Ammunition, Breastplate, Mail Skirt, Plate Helm (Open)

name: New Skills And Talents
text: The Skills and Talents below are new options for Dwarf Characters to spend XP on. These Skills and Talents cannot be used by non-Dwarf Characters unless the GM rules otherwise.

name: Blood Grudge
text: Some Grudges are much more serious than others. Grudges that demand the death of the perpetrator — those involving grievous harm, deliberate oath breaking, or monstrous creatures like Orcs, Goblins, Skaven, or followers of Chaos — are referred to as Blood Grudges. These Grudges are usually harder to settle, and impose more exacting effects on the Character when forced to interact with their perpetrators, but award more XP to Characters who successfully obtain satisfaction.

name: Grudges
text:
Amongst Dwarfs, Humans are renowned for their naive optimism. A Human, especially one confident enough to set off on adventures, views their life as a series of upcoming challenges to overcome, and makes plans based on an assumption of success. Whilst Humans look to the future, Dwarfs look to the past. They have little faith they will ever restore the fortunes of the Dwarfs’ golden age. Their priority is rarely to achieve something new, but to honour their ancestors by perpetuating the old ways… and to avenge any insults that have yet to be paid in kind.

Grudges are an alternate system for Dwarf Characters to generate XP. They supersede the rules for Ambitions detailed in WFRP Core Rulebook. A Dwarf Character can track either Grudges or Ambitions, but not both — and a party of mostly Dwarf Characters must decide if they will be using Party Grudges or Party Ambitions. Though Dwarf Characters cannot gain XP through Ambitions, they still gain XP through end-of-session rewards, adventure rewards, or bonuses at the GM’s discretion.

name: Recording Grudges
text:
A Grudge is a record of words or actions taken by another creature which have impugned a Dwarf ’s honour. Each Dwarf Character records their Grudges in a personal log, referred to as a Book of Grudges (or simply “book”). When recorded, a Grudge should specify the following:

A summary of the offence which warranted the Grudge, e.g. spilling my pint; stealing my axe; killing my brother. A Grudge is not worth recording if appropriate restitution has already been obtained, e.g. you were bought a new drink; recovered your axe; or killed the creature responsible.

The perpetrator, in as much as the Dwarf is able to identify them, e.g. Ralfa Facebruiser, the Silver Shakes gang, a goblin from the Red Eye tribe missing two front teeth. Grudges against groups, or very occasionally, inanimate objects, are also acceptable.

The restitution necessary to satisfy the Grudge. Whilst the Grudges of kings and clan leaders carefully consider appropriate restitution with reference to legal precedent, individual Dwarfs (and players) are free to set whatever restitution they consider reasonable and proportionate to the severity of the grudge.

If restitution is unreasonably low, the Dwarf may acquire a reputation as a pushover (and the player may deprive themselves of restitution benefits); if restitution is unreasonably high, the Dwarf will quickly acquire more Grudges than they are able to settle (and the player may deprive themselves of XP).

The date of the offence. You should also leave space to record the date that the Grudge is satisfied.

Once a Grudge is entered into your book, it cannot be removed except by satisfying the Grudge. Because Dwarf Characters can accumulate several Grudges over the course of their adventures, they may struggle to record all their Grudges on their character sheet. The Book of Grudges journal, sold separately, is perfect for the purpose of recording these Grudges.

name: Interacting with Perpetrators
text: Dwarfs take their Grudges extremely personally. When interacting with an individual they bear a Grudge against, they find it difficult to think of anything but getting satisfaction. When interacting with an individual you bear a Grudge against, apply the Animosity Psychology trait. When interacting with an individual you bear a Blood Grudge against, apply the Hatred Psychology trait instead. See WFRP Core Rulebook for details.

name: New Grudges
text:
At the end of each session, you can choose to gain a new Grudge. Choose an individual that insulted you during the session, and record the Grudge you bear against them per the usual process.

Unlike Ambitions, you do not need to swap a Grudge for an existing Grudge that you have completed or abandoned. For this reason, it is possible for your book of Grudges to grow over the course of a campaign.

If the entire session passes without an insult grievous enough to be entered in your book, you may still choose to enter a historic grievance as a Grudge. This refers to an incident that occurred off-screen, during downtime, or before play started, which has until this point not been relevant. As with starting Grudges, players should confer with the GM to ensure this new Grudge will have an opportunity to be pertinent during the game.

If you should endure a session of such rage-inducing offences that you wish to enter multiple Grudges into your book, you can speak to your GM about adding more than one Grudge. For each additional Grudge you add into your book, you reduce the number of Fortune points you start the next session with by 1. You cannot add more additional Grudges than you have Fortune points to spend — if you find yourself in this situation, your GM may suggest consolidating your many grievances into a single Grudge that accommodates them all.

name: Resolving Grudges
text:
Grudges are resolved when you receive the restitution listed in your book. Update the Grudge by noting the date it was satisfied in your book. If you learn that the Grudge’s perpetrator has died without making recompense, the Grudge is inherited by their closest adult relative, liege- lord, den mother, or undead master (as appropriate). A Blood Grudge is only satisfied if the perpetrator is slain by you, or allies and kin satisfying the Grudge on your behalf.

A satisfied Grudge awards 25 XP. A satisfied Blood Grudges awards an additional +25 XP, for a total of 50 XP.

name: Party Grudges
text:
If a group consists mostly of Dwarf Characters, they may choose to use Party Grudges rather than Party Ambitions. This reflects the group’s commitment to avenge wrongs paid to their party, their clan, their hold, or the Dwarf people as a whole.

Instead of choosing a Short-term Party Ambition and Long-term Party Ambition in Stage 6 of Character Creation, a group of mostly Dwarf Characters can choose to start with three Party Grudges. Any number of these can be Blood Grudges. Dwarf Characters record Party Grudges in their books individually, in exactly the same way as personal Grudges, and agree between themselves what appropriate restitution should be.

Party Grudges are resolved in the same way as personal Grudges. When all players agree the Grudge is settled, all Characters with the Grudge in their book earn 25 XP (an additional +25 XP for Blood Grudges), then marks the Grudge as satisfied. To acquire new Party Grudges, the whole group can choose to record the same Grudge as their personal Grudge for a session.

Non-Dwarf Characters in a group with Party Grudges gain XP when the Party Grudges are satisfied, in the same way as their Dwarf companions.

name: Suggested Restitution For Grudges
text:
| Type of Grudge | Suggested Restitution |
| --- | --- |
| Slander of personal honour (accusing a Dwarf of lying or shoddy craftsmanship) | An apology, as public as the insult, may suffice; compensation if the slander materially impacted earnings |
| Slander of ancestral honour ( disparaging the work of kinsfolk, or speaking ill of the dead) | A public apology, with a gratuity of gold, and efforts to affirm your ancestor’s honour |
| Material misappropriation (stealing, supplying defective goods, property damage) | Full recompense, plus gold to correct the insult, and labour to replace or repair damaged goods |
| Personal injury (suffered whilst using machinery crafted with a defect, fighting in a brawl) | Injury in kind (e.g. an eye for an eye), gold to compensate loss of earnings |
| Failure when attempting to fulfil an oath (a bodyguard’s failure to protect your kin, or cowardice in battle) | Apology and compensation from the perpetrator’s clan; perpetrator may be exiled from their clan, or swear the Slayer Oath |
| Death, torture, violation, attempted murder, or purposeful mutilation (beard trimming) of self or kinsfolk | Death of the perpetrator (see Blood Grudge); Dwarf perpetrators may be granted leniency to choose the manner of their deaths, by swearing the Slayer Oath |
| Deliberate oathbreaking (refusing to answer a lord’s call to arms, or kin-slaying) | Death of the perpetrator (see Blood Grudge); see options for leniency above |

They also gain XP from the satisfaction of a Grudge that appears in the books of all Dwarf Characters in their party. However, non-Dwarf Characters do not track Grudges in their own book, do not apply the Psychological traits of interacting with Party Grudge perpetrators, and use personal Ambitions instead of personal Grudges.

name: Unresolved Grudges
text:
Dwarfs do not subscribe to the vision of the afterlife evangelised by the priests of Morr. Instead, they believe that the spirits of their dead reside deep beneath the earth, in the Halls of the Ancestors, where they are judged by their gods and awarded a seat at the great feast table proportional to their deeds in life. It is said that Dwarfs with many Grudges left unresolved will be seated furthest from their most prestigious ancestors, and deprived of the best food and ale.

If a Dwarf Character dies, their player’s new Character starts with additional XP, equal to half the XP the deceased Character acquired in play. However, this bonus XP is reduced by 25 XP for every outstanding Grudge the deceased Character had upon death, and reduced by an additional 25 XP (50 XP total) for every outstanding Blood Grudge. If the player’s new Character considers the deceased Character to be kin, any outstanding Grudges of the deceased Character are transferred directly into the new Character’s book of Grudges.

name: Gromril armour
text:
Gromril armour is almost always only made for Dwarfs, as giving away Grungni’s gift is unthinkable to most. Only once or twice in all Dawi history has a suit been made for an outsider, that person having proven themself a true Dwarf friend. Gromril is rare, expensive, and difficult to work, but due to its unsurpassed hardness it is most commonly used in the construction of suits of armour, though such monumentally expensive suits are reserved for the mightiest Dwarf heroes and their elite tunnel fighters, the Ironbreakers.

Gromril is a legendarily durable material, the most precious metal worked by Dwarfs. Items forged from gromril will not break, corrode, or lose their edge in almost all circumstances. In addition to other qualities possessed by a piece of armour a piece of gromril armour always possesses Fine 1 and Durable 4.

Any attacks against locations protected by Gromril armour do not inflict Critical Wounds if they roll a Critical. An attack can still inflict Critical Wounds if it inflicts the target Character to 0 Wounds, as normal.

name: Gromril weapons
text:
Gromril weapons are the finest known, and only the most skilled Dwarf smiths forge weapons from it. Meant for the Dwarfkings and their elite guards, gromril weapons are also given as gifts to the great heroes of Karaz Ankor after a legendary deed. Runesmiths will often inscribe runes of power on gromril weapons, making them even more fearsome.

All gromril weapons, regardless of the presence of wounds, have the Durable 4 Quality. Axes will also have Damaging, while hammers have the Impact Quality.

To work out the price of an item made from gromril double the base cost of the item seven times. So a sword (1 GC) would cost 128 GC if made from gromril. Really, this is a minimum price for an item that somehow made its way to market. Gromril items are regarded by Dwarfs as prized military and cultural assets and they do not part with such things lightly.

name: Crewed (Rating)
text:
For this weapon to operate optimally, it must be crewed by the number of characters equal to its Rating, all with the relevant Ranged skill (e.g. a Crewed (3) weapon requires 3 trained crew to operate efficiently). Only one crewmember can fire the weapon each Round, but additional crew can move or reload the weapon in their Turn. Misfires (WFRP Core Rulebook) damage all characters crewing the weapon, to a random hit location instead of the Primary Arm.

A Crewed weapon with insufficient crew doubles its Reload Rating. In addition, the weapon gains the Imprecise Flaw if it is short 2 or more crew, and the Dangerous Flaw if it is short 3 or more crew. If this effect would duplicate Flaws the weapon already has, it inflicts −10 on Ranged Tests per duplicated Flaw.

name: Salvo (Rating)
text:
A Salvo weapon can be fired a number of times equal to its Rating before it needs to be reloaded. When shooting a Salvo weapon, you can choose to fire a single shot (reducing Salvo by 1), or a batch of missiles (reducing Salvo by the number of shots fired). Each missile fired after the first suffers a cumulative −10 on its Ranged Test (−10 for the second shot, −20 for the third shot, etc.).

The Reload Rating of a Salvo weapon indicates the SLs required to increase its Salvo by 1. A weapon’s Salvo Rating cannot exceed the number listed in its profile.

If a Dwarf Salvo weapon Misfires (WFRP Core Rulebook) on a roll of 00, the crew suffers a number of hits equal to the weapon’s remaining Salvo Rating (minimum 1).

name: Spread (Rating)
text:
Weapons with the Spread Quality fire an expanding cloud of projectiles which may strike several targets. Depending on the range to the target, weapons with this Quality behave somewhat differently.

Point Blank: The shot targets a single individual. Add (Rating) to the weapon’s Damage. Short Range to Long Range: The shot targets a single individual, and also the next (Rating) closest visible creatures. No two targets may be more than (Rating) yards apart. Extreme Range: As for Short to Long Range but reduce the weapon’s Damage by (Rating).

name: Dwarf Ammunition
text:
For ease of use, the effects that ammunition have on the Range, Damage, Qualities, and Flaws of ranged weapons have been included in the weapon profiles listed in this chapter. When replacing spent ammunition for personal weapons, Dwarfs can buy 12 bullets and powder for 3/3, and 12 crossbow bolts for 5/- (both have Common Availability). 12 shots of Drakefire can either be purchased for 1GC (Rare Availability), or concocted as an Endeavour.

Replacing ammunition for artillery is usually outside the budget of most adventuring parties. Characters determined to pay their way — or use variant ammunition like grapeshot, incendiary rounds, or animal carcasses — can find additional detail in Up in Arms (page 124).

Battle Standard: Each Dwarf clan has a banner their warriors rally behind on the battlefield. Most are topped with metal heads, hanging medallions, or other ancestor badges, so those who fight beneath them never forget their predecessors are watching and judging them. Other customisations reflect the trade of the clan — banners of mining clans mount lanterns and candles, for example. Battle standards marked with protection runes extend the range of that protection rune to 12 yards.

Metal Foil Sheets: These thin, flexible plates are used by Runescribes to inscribe a semi-permanent record — not as long-lasting as stone, but far more durable than paper.

Reckoner’s Log: The grudges a Reckoner bears on their clients’ behalf are traditionally inscribed on stone tablets, and broken once satisfied. For practical reasons, many Reckoners record their grudges on books of parchment paper instead, which reduce their Encumbrance to 1.

Stone Tablets: Despite their unwieldiness, stone tablets remain a popular choice for inscribing records that withstand the passage of time.

Trade Tools (Brewer): Pots, Buckets, Kettles, Mash Tun, Bottles, Barrels. Workshops (Breweries) include Mills, Tanks, Kegs, and Bottling Lines.

name: Dwarf Artillery
text:
A Dwarf throng rarely goes into battle without war machines to cover their advance. Like any ranged weapon, artillery can only be used if you have the right Skill Specialisation (with the exceptions noted on WFRP Core Rulebook). Catapults are a new Weapon Group that can only be used if you have the Ranged (Catapult) Skill. Unlike Human Engineering weapons, not every Dwarf Engineering weapon uses blackpowder — the Blackpowder and Damaging

Qualities only apply to Engineering weapons if explicitly listed in their profile.

The Dawi were the first to use gunpowder for anything beyond fireworks. Even before Cathay, Karaz Ankor was deploying not just arquebuses and swivel guns, but heavy cannon for defence of their holds. While some see use on the battlefield, others are fixed in place to defend mountain pass and fortress gates. Ever inventive, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr have even found a way to use heavy explosives underwater. All weapons in this section require a crew of three and the Ranged (Engineering) Skill. For each crew member lacking the appropriate skill, or for every skilled crew member below the required number, the Test is made at a (-10) penalty.

name: Bombard
text: A small cannon that fires lead shot the size of a Dawi’s fist, Dwarfs value the bombard for delivering a punch while still easily portable. A crew of two Dwarfs can carry it to a new location and set it up in 1d3 rounds. It can then be fired on the next round. Both gunners must have the Ranged (Bombard) Skill. A single crewman can operate the bombard, but not move it, and the reload time is doubled.

name: Cannon
text: The typical artillery piece of Karaz Ankor’s armies, the cannon is similar to those used by the Empire, an unsurprising fact given the assistance of Imperial Dwarfs in the gunnery school at Nuln. They are, however, more reliable, as the Karaz Ankor Engineers Guild is fond of pointing out. A Dwarf field cannon only misfires on an even-numbered double that is also a failed roll. Barak Varr makes use of a somewhat larger version on its heavy ships, called the ‘Tempest’ cannon, with 50% greater range and an additional D+2.

name: Mortar
text: Squat like a Dwarf, the mortar is a short-barreled cannon meant for indirect fire. Launching a cannonball on a high, arching trajectory, it can hit targets otherwise protected by being behind buildings, forests, or fortifications. While a line of sight to the target is not necessary, all shots from a mortar are a Hard (-20) Test, unless there is a spotter to relay precise information about the target. The mortar crew consists of two Dwarfs, each of whom has the Ranged (Mortar) Skill.

name: Swivel Gun
text: Sometimes called the ‘Halfling’s Cannon’, the swivel gun is somewhere between a large blunderbuss and a small artillery weapon. It consists of two pieces, the gun itself and a heavy, collapsible tripod as a mount. When loaded, it can fire almost any shot, from a single small cannonball to multiple small lead bullets to even rocks. When firing multiple projectiles, the swivel gun has the Blast (2) Quality. Effective use of the swivel gun requires two trained crew with the Ranged (Swivel Gun) Skill, one to fire the gun, the other to set up the tripod. Of limited use on the open battlefield, the swivel gun is popular for use in tunnels, defending fortifications from assault, and as anti-personnel weapons on the ships of Barak Varr.

name: Volley Gun
text: Rather than a cranked circle of tubes, as with Imperial volley Guns, the Dwarf volley gun is a smaller, more ‘intimate’ version of the organ gun. It fires a blast of lead musket balls from up to ten barrels at once. Often mounted on a wheeled carriage for mobility on the battlefield, the volley gun serves to savagely rip through a charging enemy before they can come into contact with the Dwarf lines. The volley gun requires a crew of two with the Ranged (Blackpowder) Skill. A crew of one can fire it with no penalty, but the reload time is doubled, nor can it be moved.

name: Aerial Bombs
text: Both Gyrocopters and war Balloons can carry aerial bombs. Though less powerful than a standard bomb, several raining from above can still terrorise an enemy. As a dropped weapon, the bomb’s range is irrelevant. Aerial bombs are smaller, however, and so do less damage.

name: Breaker Cannon
text: The breaker is the standard gun on Barak Varr’s ships and is a lighter version of the field cannon. There have been experiments with dismounting these guns and taking them ashore with Dwarf landing parties that move out of range of a ship’s guns, but this is still considered an insufficiently tested innovation.

name: Brimstone Gun
text: Since the development of drakefire, some Gyrocopter pilots have exchanged their Steam Gun for this new armament — preferring to take the risk on newer technology for the advantage of improved range and stopping power.

name: Steam Gun
text: Originally designed to relieve pressure on a Gyrocopter’s steam engine, the Engineers Guild quickly realised the military applications for an expanding cloud of scalding water vapour. Before discharging a Steam Gun, Gyrocopter pilots must carefully position their vehicle to compensate for the weapon’s short range, whilst still avoiding retaliation from the blistered survivors.

name: Tempest Cannon
text: Barak Varr makes use of a somewhat larger version on its heavy ships, called the ‘Tempest’ cannon, with 50% greater range and an additional D+2.

name: Thunder Cannon
text: The thunder cannon is the largest gun Karaz Ankor produces, so heavy that it cannot travel with an army. Instead, this cannon guards the gates and mountain passes leading to the Dwarf Empire’s holds. Mounted in fortified casements on the sides of mountains, its crew of five operates carefully engineered clockworks and steam- powered hydraulics to control its aim and elevation. In addition to the Ranged (Engineering) Skill to fire, properly operating the aiming mechanisms requires a successful Challenging (+0) Trade (Engineering) Test. On a failure, each -1 SL counts as a -10 penalty to the Ranged (Engineering) Test.

Operators may be required to Test when moving at accelerated speeds, negotiating difficult terrain, attempting an unusual manoeuvre, or engaging in a dangerous pursuit.

Vehicles suffer Damage in the same way as Characters. Their Toughness Bonus reduces the amount of Damage taken, and their Wounds indicate much Damage they can withstand before destruction. Attacks against vehicles usually gain a bonus due to the vehicle’s Enormous or Monstrous Size, and in melee are opposed by the driver’s Drive, Row, or Sail Skill (as appropriate). If a melee attack is made against a stationary vehicle, or a vehicle the attacker is on board, the defender does not roll and counts as scoring –10 SL. The effects of Criticals, or called shots, should be improvised according to the vehicle’s specific components — you’ll find suggestions throughout this chapter.

Lasting repairs to a vehicle require specialist facilities and a team of professionals, but a Character with appropriate Trade Tools can implement temporary repairs. This is a Difficult (−10) Trade (Engineering) Test (or other relevant Trade Specialisation) to restore 1d10+SL Wounds to the vehicle, or undo the effects of a Critical. These problems return at the end of the adventure.

Several WFRP supplements provide more detailed vehicle rules, including additional Critical effects, customisation options, the impact of weather or other hazards, and Endeavours suitable for long-distance vehicle travel. If you would like to furnish your vehicles with this additional level of detail, recommended supplements include the Enemy in Shadow Companion (for land vehicles), Enemy in Ruins (for air vehicles), and Sea of Claws (for water vehicles).

name: Vehicle Rules
text: The steamcraft, skycraft, and watercraft in this chapter all use the same vehicle profile. Vehicle Crew indicates the number of trained individuals required to operate the vehicle effectively. Encumbrance measures the weight and bulk of the vehicle itself. Carry Capacity states how many Encumbrance points of cargo the vehicle can easily hold (all vehicle handling Tests suffer a –1 penalty for each 10% by which this capacity is exceeded). Movement details how many yards-per-Turn it moves in combat, and miles-per-hour for long distance travel. Testing Drive, Row, or Sail is usually unnecessary when travelling.

name: Earth Borer Mining Drill
text:
Grindolsson’s original design called for a gigantic steel drill bit mounted on a heavy cannon carriage whose wheels could be locked in place. A steam engine also mounted on the carriage would turn the drill, though the borer itself had to be wheeled into position by hand. A tragic accident that led to the deaths of several Dwarfs showed the dangers of the drill overheating, thus a crew was added to run a pump and spray water on the drill to cool it.

Dwarf engineers eventually worked out a complex mechanism to use the steam engine to also drive the wheels and power a built-in water cooling pump, making the Earth Borer self-propelled. This reduced the crew needed for each borer from a dozen Dwarfs to just four. Crews now compete with each other to see who can dig the deepest new tunnels the fastest.

While digging tunnels to find new resources, it was inevitable that Earth Borer crews would encounter Skaven. The first response was to armour the carriage to protect the crew, but soon the Dawi thought of offensive uses. Building larger, extended versions of the Earth Borer, Dwarf Engineers turned them into troop carriers and assault vehicles. Able to carry up to a dozen armoured

Dwarfs in addition to the crew, the ‘War Borers’ are used to raid Skaven lairs, surprising them by attacking from new directions through freshly dug tunnels. The latest models can even drop explosives to collapse tunnels as the borer withdraws at the end of a raid.

Earth Borers with a Drill Bit can carve a path directly through solid rock, though they reduce their Move to 1 whilst doing so. A Critical hit against an Earth Borer jams its drilling mechanism, immobilising its progress through the earth, and overloading its steam boiler if the jam is not cleared.

name: What’S Mine Is Mine
text:
Dawi have strong ideas about property rights, especially when it comes to the products of their own craftsmanship and labour. When a Dwarf spends years making a complex piece of technology, from a submersible to a gyrocopter to a musket, making it not only functional, but beautiful, it becomes something very personal to them. Each Dwarf Engineer, therefore, feels a very real sense of ownership over his creation and is reluctant to hand it over to another, unless it was a commissioned work, or ordered to do so at the command of a Dwarfking. Dwarfs have a hard time describing it, but tell Humans to imagine giving away a part of their own body. This conflict was at the heart of Dargo Grindolsson’s anguish.

But this possessiveness does not apply to everything. Common, everyday items do not evoke this response. Thus Humans who have heard wild tales of the Dwarfs’ legendary greed are surprised when a Dwarf has no problem letting them borrow a hammer. They are equally surprised when the Dwarf reacts in outrage at an offer to buy their handcrafted blunderbuss.

Dwarf Skycraft are piloted with the Sail (Skycraft) Skill (page 80). Unlike other vehicles, the experimental nature of skycraft dictates that the pilot must always take an Average (+20) Sail (Skycraft) Test during take-off and landing, with failed Tests delaying arrival/departure, or inflicting damage on the vehicle/its occupants/the landing zone. A Critical hit against a flying vehicle results in a sudden loss of altitude — startling and nauseating the crew at best, triggering a crash with nearby terrain at worst.

name: Gyrocopter and variants
text:
’It’s just like riding a horse, except you don’t usually get back on after falling off.’

—A Dawi gyrocopter pilot to an Imperial cavalryman

One of the Dwarfs’ most ingenious inventions, the gyrocopter evokes wonder from all who see it, as well as exclamations of shock and awe.

Gyrocopters are an invention of the Dwarf Engineers’ Guild. As the legend goes, the inventor was inspired by the sight of a Dragon swooping over the Worlds Edge Mountains. He thought that the engines used to drive steam-powered drilling machinery might provide the necessary thrust, and that adapting flywheels from grinding machines would help power and stabilise the device. His invention proved successful, and whilst it has been much adapted and refined over the centuries since, the basic principles are still employed in the more recent designs. Now only the smaller Dwarf holds or more conservative clans fail to keep a small fleet of Gyrocopters., Because of the time and skill required to make one, as well as the Dawi’s adherence to a workshop model of production, the Dwarfs produce relatively few gyrocopters, and those few are risked sparingly. While now in use in Karaz Ankor and some of the Western holds, the gyrocopter has never been willingly given or sold to an outsider.

The typical gyrocopter is an open frame of metal and wood with a seat for one pilot, who also operates the steam cannon. Fueled by a highly-efficient coal, a small steam engine powers the propellers used for lift and steering, and also generates steam for the cannon. Before takeoff, the engine is primed with enough coal to last eight hours, or four if repeated use is made of the steam cannon.

Gyrocopters take-off vertically, and are capable of hovering in place. Most are equipped with a Steam Gun, but some variants replace this weapon with a Brimstone Gun, or strip out the weapon entirely (which increases its Move to 25). The craft’s stabilisers are also fitted with a small payload of Aerial Bombs.

Gyrobombers are heavier, double-rotored versions of the Gyrocopter, their increased size improving their capacity for munitions. Most are equipped with bouncing, multi- explosive Grudgebuster Bomb racks, and a lighter Clattergun in place of the Gyrocopter’s main weapon. Occasionally, a Gryobomber may be stripped of its bomb racks, and used to deliver emergency relief supplies to besieged holds — this increases its Carry Capacity to 60.

Though it is fuel-intensive, all Gyrocopters can achieve incredible bursts of speed in combat, moving up to 5 times their Move with a Challenging (+0) Sail (Skycraft) Test. Failed Tests may place unexpected pressure upon the vehicle’s steam engine, resulting in reduced acceleration or loss of altitude. See the Flight Creature Trait (WFRP Core Rulebook) for more guidelines about flying combatants, though Gyrocopters cannot take-off and land in combat without expending a Move to do so.

The success of the gyrocopter has spawned variations geared to a specific purpose. The ‘fast’ gyrocopter is a model built for speed. With no cannon or bombs and made of lighter material, it is 25% faster than the standard gyrocopter, but with a Toughness of only 5. Its primary use is for reconnaissance and carrying urgent messages between holds.

A heavier, slower model is lovingly called ‘Pack Mule’ by its pilots and those to whom it brings needed supplies. Larger than standard, usually unarmed, and with a more powerful steam engine, the undercarriage is fitted with a hook that lets the craft lift a pallet or crate slung by ropes. It can carry up to 300 Enc of packed goods, 250 if armed, but flies 25% slower than the standard gyrocopter.

name: Aerial Bombs
text: Both Gyrocopters and war Balloons can carry aerial bombs. Though less powerful than a standard bomb, several raining from above can still terrorise an enemy. As a dropped weapon, the bomb’s range is irrelevant. Aerial bombs are smaller, however, and so do less damage.

name: War Balloon
text:
The earliest Dwarf aerial vehicle was the balloon. First used at Karak Kadrin in the War of Vengeance to keep an eye out for Elves, they proved their worth in the aftermath of the Skaven and greenskin invasions. Observers posted in tethered outposts high above the approaches to the mountains kept watch and sent warnings to the holds below via message cylinder or semaphore. Eventually an Engineer clan tried adding a small steam engine and propeller, this giving rise to the ‘War Balloon’.

The War Balloon is simply a gondola of wicker and light metal suspended beneath a balloon by guy ropes that also form a net to hold the balloon’s shape. When powered with an engine and propeller, it is capable of slow flight, even against all but the strongest winds, and carries coal for a week’s travel. This enables the War Balloon to go on scouting missions far beyond the edges of the World’s Edge Mountains through a judicious use of the winds and the steam engine. War Balloons are primarily used for surveillance and reconnaissance, and are painted in neutral colours that blend into the sky, imposing a –20 modifier on enemy Perception Tests to spot them. Their maximum altitude is much higher than a Gyrocopter, and they can be tethered in mid-air when the weather is agreeable. Despite their name, War Balloons are rarely heavily armed, but may carry a complement of Aerial Bombs, along with Handguns and Crossbows for the crew.

name: Watercraft
text:
’A key to keeping our remaining tanks in good working order may be in understanding the watercraft of the Dwarfs. They are clad in similar grade and thickness of steel, mount far more artillery, and are similarly propelled through the power of a steam engine. I am sure Miragliano must have had the Ironclad and Monitor in mind when he drafted blueprints for his own land ship. If only the Engineers’ Guilds of our erstwhile allies could be persuaded to share their ideas it might provide our salvation.’

— Engineer Commander Feinkopf, in a lucid moment

Dwarf ships, let alone a whole armed fleet, are just inconceivable to most people outside Karaz Ankor. The idea that a folk so rooted in the earth, so dedicated to digging ever deeper, could even want to sail the seas, let alone build ships for it, seems laughable on its face.

And yet building a navy is exactly what one Dwarf hold has done.

The Hold of Barak Varr is an outlier from the rest of Karaz Ankor in more ways than one. One of the southernmost holds remaining after the fall of Karak Drazh and Karak

Instead it sits in the Varenka Hills, where the Skull river flows into the Black Gulf, against the lands of the Border Princes. Some Dawi in the other holds claim this gives the Dwarfs of Barak Varr a strange outlook, more manling than Dwarf.

Regardless, the reality of the lands and waters around Barak Varr, as well as the dangers they faced, led them to become very good shipbuilders.

Isolated in the Varenka Hills, Barak Varr’s only connection to the rest of Karaz Ankor is along the Skull River. This waterway flows from a source near the road from Karaz- A-Karak to Black Fire Pass and enters the Black Gulf near Barak Varr. Though necessary, travel along the river is unsafe, thanks to the dangers posed by raiding greenskins and Humans from the Border Princes.

The Black Gulf is itself dangerous. Raiders of all sorts have tried to assault Barak Varr from the sea, ranging from Sartosan pirates to the fleet of Skaven that terrorised the coasts along the Gulf and the Great Ocean in 2231 IC. Facing threats no army could touch, Barak Varr decided to build an ‘army of the sea’.

Throwing themselves into the task, the Engineers and workshops of the hold studied captured ships and learned all they could from them. And then they improved them, building a range of ships from those meant for rivers to great steel craft that could travel on and under the Black Gulf. They adapted their weapons for use on the water and invented ones for battles beneath the waves.

Unique among the peoples of the Old World, the oceangoing ships of the Dwarfs, the Monitors, Ironclads, Dreadnoughts, and submersibles, are all metal, defying and baffling the shipbuilders of other kingdoms. Like other powerful weapons of the Dwarfs, each ship is an individual work of craftsmanship by a Master Naval Engineer of Barak Varr and his apprentices, and experienced sailors can identify not only the type of ship, but the workshop it came from based on its design.

All Dwarf ships are steam powered, sails having been abandoned once centuries of testing (and letting others take the risks) had shown that they were reliable and could be scaled to the needs of a large craft. Rejecting the propellers that worked so well on airships, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr instead chose to power all their ships save the Nautilus by paddlewheel — a small sternwheel on the river gunboats and great side wheels on the oceangoing ships. Dwarf ships are thus not dependent on the wind.

Unlike the ships of Humans and Elves, which have open decks and are exposed to the elements, Barak Varr’s metal ships are also completely sealed, from keel to crow’s nest. Access to the crew areas and the storage holds are only through tightly sealed hatches that can be barred from the inside. Not only watertight, this design also keeps out boarders — since the first Ironclads were launched in the 18th century IC, no enemy has ever successfully boarded and captured a Dwarf ocean ship.

Barak Varr’s ships are equipped to fight at range and up close. The guns of all ships except the gunboat are mounted in sealed turrets to protect the gun crews, while hydraulic mechanisms powered by the ship’s steam plant allows the turret to rotate as needed. This lets the ship swiftly bring its guns to bear on an enemy, rather than turn the entire hull.

Like their land-bound cousins, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr like to get up close and personal in a fight. All Dwarf ships other than the gunboat are equipped with steel rams meant to punch holes in the enemy’s wooden hulls, the Dwarf ship pulling back and striking again and again until the enemy sinks. Few captains have the courage — or are sufficiently insane — to face an oncoming Ironclad as its steamwhistle bellows a challenge.

Rams play a role in boarding actions, too. When a captain decides it is better to capture a ship as a prize than sink it, he rams it once to hold it in place. Then the crew swing a hydraulic ramp into place, across which a squad of axe and hammer-wielding Dwarfs charge to seize the other vessel. Many see it as proof that Dwarfs who go to sea are ‘not quite right in the head’, because they charge in full armour — over the open ocean!

Dwarf Watercraft are piloted with the Sail Skill. Each Watercraft has its own Specialisation, but a Character with Advances in any Sail Specialisation treats all other Sail Specialisations as Basic Skills. Critical hits against boats might inflict penalties to Sail Tests, deal 9 Damage to occupants due to flying splinters, or even cause the boat to take on water.

name: Gunboat
text:
Vital to their trade with Karaz-a-Karak and the rest of Karaz Ankor beyond it, the Dwarfs of Barak Varr fought hard to secure the route for its trade barges. Under threat from greenskins and Trolls, as well as less-than- neighbourly petty rulers among the Border Princes, the Dwarfkings found themselves forced to devote large numbers of warriors to protect the barges, both coming and going. Even then, losses could be heavy.

Tasked by the Dwarfking to ‘do something’, in the 19th century IC the Engineers of Barak Varr came up with the ‘Gunboat’. An armour-clad, steam-driven ship the size of an Imperial patrol boat, about 25 feet long, the gunboat mounts its engine amidships for greater efficiency as it drives twin paddlewheels, one on each side. Gunboats usually carry a crew of eight — a captain, a pilot and his relief, four gunners, and an engineer to maintain the engine — but can carry up to a half-dozen more Dwarfs, if the threats warrant it. Regardless of crew numbers, all Dwarfs on a gunboat are trained warriors, ready to fight in addition to their other duties. To provide shelter at night, Barak Varr maintains a variety of fortified inn, the walls of which also provide protection to docked rivercraft, about a day’s travel from each other. Surrounded by often-hostile country, visitors other than Dwarfs are a rare sight.

On escort duty or patrol, gunboats frequently travel in pairs for mutual support. Protecting a convoy, one will lead a group of barges, while the other brings up the rear, both on constant watch for ambushes. If on patrol and the need arises to check something onshore, one boat will stay on watch, while the crew of the other investigates. Barak Varr often sends small patrols such as these up the tributaries of the Skull and Blood rivers to make sure no threats are building in the ‘backcountry’.

Gunboats mount a ram on the prow, which provides 5 Armour Points, and can be used to effectively neutralise boats of similar size by smashing into them. All other parts of the Gunboat have 2 Armour Points of protection.

Each Gunboat mounts two turrets, which can be a Swivel Gun or Volley Gun. The forward gun rests in a ‘gun pit’ with a 180 degree firing arc, which provides hard cover to the crew (a –30 hit modifier on ranged attacks). The rear gun is on a raised platform with a 360 firing arc, providing medium cover (a –20 modifier on ranged attacks).

name: Steam Barge
text:
Prior to the steam engine, barges travelling between Karaz Ankor and the Karaz-a-Karak road had to be towed upstream by mule teams, or even by gangs of Dawi pulling on tow ropes. This made the trips even more dangerous and costly, as the craft and their crews were vulnerable to attack. In times of turmoil, losses could be high, and the risk was always present that Barak Varr could be cut off from Karaz Ankor.

Along with the gunboat, then, the hold’s Engineers developed a steam-powered barge that allowed each barge to be manned by fewer crew and travel in the middle of the river, farther from dangerous shores. Propelled by a single paddlewheel at the rear, the steam barge is a flat platform 30 feet in length and 10 feet wide, with low walls around the deck. The deck supports two small cabins, one at the rear for the engine and paddlewheel mechanism, the other in the middle for the crew. The usual crew consists of a captain, the Engineer, and two labourer Dwarfs. A reversed tiller at the bow controls two rudders used for steering.

Other than the cabins, the deck is open for the carrying of cargo. When not powering the wheel, the steam engine is used to operate a collapsible crane for loading and unloading cargo in nets. With careful loading, the capacity of a steam barge is much greater than that of a large Imperial river barge, 800 Enc.

Unarmoured, slow, and with only personal weapons for the crew, the steam barge is not made for combat. Instead, travelling in convoys of up to five barges, it relies on the protection of the escorting gunboats during the day and the fortified inns at night.

name: Dreadnought
text:
The Dreadnought is the latest evolution of Barak Varr’s surface ships, an immense warship capable of sinking an entire enemy flotilla on its own. With the farthest range of any Dwarf warship as well as awesome size and armament, the Kings of Barak Varr have often chosen the Dreadnought to ‘show the colours’ in other lands, whenever necessary to impress — or intimidate — outsiders.

Three great paddlewheels, one on each side and a larger one at the stern, propel the Dreadnoughts the length of the Black Gulf and far out into the Southern Sea. A great engine room, more complex and powerful than any yet designed by Barak Varr’s naval workshops, powers the wheels and the ships turrets and steering system. More heavily armed than any previous class of Dwarf ship, there are two turrets each fore and aft, one in each pair mounted above and behind the other. Each turret mounts a pair of Thunder cannon — a salvo from these is so powerful, it would roll or tear apart any ship less massive than a Dreadnought. Two smaller turrets higher up toward the bridge each support a single Tempest cannon, while five Breaker cannons on each side add to a broadside. Rounding out its armaments, like Ironclads, the Dreadnought has small ports used for anti-personnel fire against enemy ships.

Dreadnoughts have 2 Armour Points of protection to all locations. At the fore and aft, two turrets bear two Thunder Cannons each, for eight Thunder Cannons in total. Each pair of turrets is positioned so that one is above and behind the other. Towards the bridge, two higher, smaller turrets bear a Tempest Cannon each, and five Breaker Cannons on each side provide a broadside. Like Ironclads, Dreadnoughts have small ports used for anti-personnel fire against enemy ships.

Alternate weapon configurations are common, to suit the preferences of the Engineer who crafted it, and the Admiral in command. For example, Grudgebreaker-class battleships mount only one turret of three Thunder Cannons, to make space for the launch pad of a small combat dirigible.

name: Ironclad
text:
Larger, more stable, and more heavily armed and armoured than a Monitor, the Ironclad is the mainstay of Barak Varr’s fleet, able to project power far out to sea or other lands.

Dual paddlewheels, one on each side and each powered by its own engine, provide the Ironclad with after turns and much more manoeuvrability overall than not only a Monitor, but the ships of other species and nations. Crewed by 75 to 100 Dwarfs, Ironclads have two enclosed turrets, fore and aft. Each mount a battery of two Tempest cannons, while above and behind each of these is a secondary battery of one Breaker, each. Casements on each side provide space for a further four Breakers, each.

Ironclads also have many small gun ports on each side for use during boarding actions, when the covering hatches are dropped and crew-dwarfs can sweep the enemy decks with swivel guns, volley guns, or even crossbows.

Ironclads have 2 Armour Points of protection to all locations, with enclosed turrets to the fore and aft. Each mounts a battery of two Tempest Cannons, with a Breaker Cannon above and behind each turret. Casements provide space for a further four Breaker Cannons on each side. Ironclads also have many small gun ports on each side for use during boarding actions, when the covering hatches are dropped and crew can sweep the enemy decks with swivel guns, volley guns, or crossbows.

name: Monitor
text:
Monitors were the firsts ships designed at Barak Varr, and were a response to the threat of pirates and other raiders to coastal shipping. They operate in and just beyond the Blood River delta and guard the approaches to Barak Varr, as well as the coasts as far west as the River Treblecz and the allied manling port of Somjek, and as far south as a day’s sailing from the hold.

The steel hull sits low in the water, supporting a squat, enclosed top castle affectionately referred to as the ‘turtle’. From this arises both the funnel for the steam engine, which powers a single rear paddlewheel, and a gunnery turret that can rotate through a 270 degrees arc, its only ‘blind spot’ being where the funnel sits behind it.

Crewed by 20-25 Dwarfs, Monitors are capable of attacking at range and by ramming. The turret mounts two cannon, usually Breakers, but some are field testing switching one for a flame cannon for use against wooden ships. Beyond the turret guns, Monitors are armed with up to five Breaker cannons on each side, for a formidable broadside.

Their low freeboard limits their seaworthiness, however, as rough weather can swamp them. Monitors thus mainly serve a coastal defence role. To project power further out to sea, Barak Varr developed the Ironclad. Monitors are fitted with a ram, a turret, and 2 Armour Points of protection (as Gunboats). The turret usually mounts two Breaker Cannons, but replacing one with a Flame Cannon is a popular choice for use against wooden ships. Beyond the turret guns, Monitors are armed with up to five Breaker cannons on each side, for a formidable broadside.

name: Nautilus Submersible
text:
The oddest class of ship in Barak Varr’s fleet, the Nautilus steam submersible is capable of travelling both on and below the surface of the water. When on the surface, it resembles nothing so much as a Monitor, but with two turrets, one fore and aft, each housing a single Breaker cannon. Instead of a ram, two torpedo tubes are mounted in the bow. The only ship not to use paddlewheels, submersibles move by means of dual screws.

The Nautilus’s most notable feature is its ability to submerge under the waves, travel underwater, and stay there for extended periods of time. When the captain gives the order, the crew seals the hatches tight, opens a set of valves and floods the ballast tanks in the hull. With a trained crew, a submersible can vanish beneath the waves in less than a minute. To surface, air from compressed tanks is forced into the ballast tanks, pushing the water out.

Nautilus Submersibles are armed with two Breaker Cannon turrets (fore and aft), with two Nautilus Torpedoes ready to fire from a pair of tubes mounted in the bow.

The Nautilus can safely dive to a depth of 30 yards, and stay there for up to one hour. Whilst underwater, it reduces its Move to 2, and cannot fire its Breaker Cannons. However, it may still fire its Nautilus Torpedoes, and is effectively immune to enemy fire — unless the enemy has a means to launch underwater attacks, or can force the submersible to resurface.

After one hour, the effects of oxygen depletion and boiler fumes begin to suffocate the Nautilus’ crew (WFRP Core Rulebook), unless the vessel resurfaces for at least three hours. Consequently, Nautilus captains prefer to travel on the surface, diving only when absolutely necessary.

A Nautilus Submersible can push itself to greater depths of 30 yards, but doing so places extraordinary pressure upon the vessel’s hull. The Nautilus makes a Challenging (+0) Toughness Test every 10 minutes or so it spends at lower depths, with increased difficulties for extreme depths. If the Test is failed, the vehicle suffers 30 Wounds from springing leaks and the buckling hull. A trained crew can make Sail (Nautilus) and Trade (Engineer) Tests to anticipate the submersible’s limits, safely resurfacing before Toughness Tests become necessary.

Submersibles normally have a crew complement of 20, but finding sufficient crew can sometimes be difficult. While the Dwarfs of Barak Varr can overcome the traditional Dawi aversion to not being on or under land, the idea of going under the water is too much for most. The assumption is that a Dwarf must be somewhat unhinged to actually want to do this.

But there are Dwarfs daring and even reckless enough to do this. Joining a Nautilus crew, where casualties can be high, is for some an alternative to expiating shame by taking the Slayer’s oath. Indeed, the King of Barak Varr has formally offered the choice of submersible service, instead of becoming a Slayer, a proposition that has been learned of and taken up by others of distant holds.
